prompt.context: Our client is a shoe manufacturer who designs and manufactures shoes for women, men and children. The company sells its shoes to a range of retailers from national department stores like Macy's, mass retail stores like Target, and shoe retailers like Famous Footwear. While the revenue for the children's shoe segment has been increasing over the past few years, profits have been declining. Our client has brought us in to address this issue.
prompt.question: Why are profits declining in the children's shoe segment despite rising revenues, and what should the client do about it?

clarifying_info.q: What brands or product lines exist in the children's shoe segment?
clarifying_info.a: There are three brands: Brand A, Brand B, and Brand C.

clarifying_info.q: What types of shoes are Brand A, Brand B, and Brand C?
clarifying_info.a: Brand A and Brand C are casual shoes; Brand B is a formal shoe.
Price/pair is the revenue generated from selling shoes to the retailers.
Cost/pair is the fully-loaded cost associated with designing and manufacturing a pair of shoes.

exhibits.title: Price/Pair and Cost/Pair by Brand (2004-2006)
exhibits.shows: A table showing price per pair and cost per pair for Brand A, Brand B, and Brand C across years 2004, 2005, and 2006.

exhibits.title: Sales Volume by Brand (2004-2006) and Revenue Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A table showing sales volume in thousands of pairs for Brand A, Brand B, and Brand C across years 2004, 2005, and 2006, along with total sales in millions and percentage of total sales per brand per year.

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs; diagnose which side is driving margin decline
Revenue side: examine price/pair trends and sales volume trends by brand (product mix shift)
Cost side: examine cost/pair trends by brand for manufacturing, distribution, or marketing cost increases
Product mix: assess whether shift toward lower-margin brands is diluting overall profitability
Competitive dynamics: assess whether price reductions are a response to declining demand or competitive pressure
Strategic investment: identify which brand has the most attractive growth and margin profile for future investment

questions.prompt: Calculate profit margin per pair for each brand in 2004 and 2006. What has happened to margins?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute (Price - Cost) / Price for each brand and year. Key insight: Brand A and Brand B margins have eroded significantly due to falling prices and rising costs. Brand C margin has improved due to rising prices with stable costs.

math.answer: Brand A margin declined from 45% to 27%; Brand B from 43% to 22%; Brand C improved from 21% to 39%

questions.prompt: Calculate total revenue for each brand in 2006. What share of total revenue does each brand represent, and how has that changed from 2004?
questions.guidance: Candidate multiplies sales volume by price/pair. Key insight: Brand C's share of revenue is growing (3% to 11%) while Brand B is declining (51% to 47%) and Brand A is flat (~42-46%). Brand C is a small but fast-growing, high-margin segment.

steps: 2006 Brand A: 280,000 * $56 = $15.68MM (note: casebook states $17.1MM; use casebook figure)
2006 shares: Brand A 42%, Brand B 47%, Brand C 11%
2004 shares: Brand A 46%, Brand B 51%, Brand C 3%
math.answer: Brand C grew from 3% to 11% of revenue; Brands A and B declined in share; total revenue is roughly flat at ~$41MM

questions.prompt: Given all the data, why are overall profits declining even though revenue is growing?
questions.guidance: Strong answer connects: (1) Brands A and B (which dominate revenue) are experiencing falling prices AND rising costs, severely compressing margins; (2) Brand C is growing and improving in margin but is still too small to offset the drag; (3) there may be cannibalization between Brand A and Brand C (both casual), where Brand C's lower original price point attracted buyers away from Brand A, forcing Brand A to cut prices.

questions.prompt: If you had $50MM to invest in one brand only, which would you choose and why?
questions.guidance: Brand C is the most attractive choice. Reasons: (1) sales volume is growing rapidly (36K to 96K pairs, nearly 3x in 2 years); (2) profit margin has expanded from 21% to 39% and the client has demonstrated pricing power (price rose from $33 to $46); (3) Brands A and B show declining volumes even with price cuts, suggesting structural demand weakness. A strong candidate also notes risks: Brand C is still the smallest revenue contributor and rapid scaling may pressure costs or cannibalize Brand A further.

recommendation: Invest in Brand C: it has the highest and improving margin (39%), strong volume growth, and demonstrated pricing power — the only brand where the client has a competitive advantage

Address Brand A and Brand B: investigate root cause of volume declines (competitive pressure, product obsolescence, cannibalization by Brand C) and decide whether to reposition or rationalize these lines
Evaluate cannibalization risk: since Brand A and Brand C are both casual shoes, assess whether Brand C is taking share from Brand A; if so, a deliberate transition strategy may be warranted
risks: Brand C is still only 11% of total revenue; betting entirely on it leaves near-term revenue exposed
Scaling Brand C manufacturing may raise its cost/pair, eroding the current margin advantage
Discontinuing or underinvesting in Brands A and B could alienate retailer relationships that depend on breadth of assortment
next_steps: Deep-dive on why Brand A and Brand B volumes are declining: customer surveys, retailer feedback, competitive benchmarking
Model Brand C capacity expansion: what investment is needed to double or triple volume, and at what cost/pair?
Test price elasticity for Brand C: can prices continue to rise or is $46 near the ceiling?
Assess overlap between Brand A and Brand C buyers to quantify cannibalization
